title: Sparse Planning in Visual World Models via Cost Gradients
claim: Importance scores derived from the downstream planning-cost gradient let us select a fixed sparse token subset once, then plan only on it.
layout: 2 stacked stages, left-to-right flow, dashed backprop arrow looping over the top
description: A two-part flow diagram. The top part, (a), starts at an Observation image on the left and passes it through a DINOv2 encoder to a grid of tokens z. These go through a Full WM block with a0=0 to a predicted token grid, then into an orange Goal cost box. A Goal image goes through its own DINOv2 encoder and feeds the same cost box. A dashed orange arrow labeled 'Backpropagate to input tokens' runs along the top back to z. Below, the gradient scores s_j = ||∇ L_plan||_2 appear as a teal-shaded grid. A Top-K arrow turns that grid into a sparse selected set S. A teal line leads down to part (b), 'Plan on the selected tokens'. It has three boxes in a row: Fixed selected tokens, Sparse CEM planning, and Execute first action. A footer note reads 'Same subset across candidates and iterations'. Blue-gray is used for the token grids and orange for the gradient path. Teal marks the selected tokens.
caption: \rev{\textbf{\costgrad{}: select once, then plan on the selected tokens.} (a) A full-token, zero-action probe supplies planning-cost gradients to select top-$K$ positions $\mathcal S$ for context and goal. (b) CEM searches for actions using only $\mathcal S$, then executes the first action. The subset stays fixed throughout action search and is reselected at the next observation; model weights remain frozen. Token grids are schematic; proprioception is omitted.}
abstract: Token-based world models enable fine-grained latent planning, but repeatedly processing large spatial token grids makes action search expensive. We introduce COSTGRAD, a training-free, goal-conditioned selector that ranks spatial tokens by the gradient norm of the planning cost with respect to each input token. By deriving importance from the downstream control objective, COSTGRAD targets tokens that matter for planning rather than merely for prediction. On AdaLN-conditioned predictors at $50\%$ sparsity, COSTGRAD matches or exceeds full-token planning on three of four continuous-control benchmarks, while giving a measured $2.6\times$ wall-clock speedup per environment planning step. Combining token sparsity with reduced CEM search increases this to a $\sim 5\times$ total speedup while still exceeding the full-token baseline. We also identify an architecture-dependent failure mode: in a matched AdaLN-vs-concat comparison, concat maintains comparable full-token performance but pure COSTGRAD loses its advantage over random selection. This difference tracks action-pathway drift: gradient-selected removal produces less drift than random removal on AdaLN, but more on concat. These results highlight selector-architecture compatibility as a design axis for sparse world-model planning. Project page and demos: https://ycxuyingchen.github.io/costgrad/
